text: Literature is concentrated by organism: Homo sapiens accounts for 46.7% of gene-paper records; the top five account for 72.8%; the top 1,000 of 20,723 organisms with literature account for 94.2%.
quote: *Homo sapiens* alone accounts for **46.7%** of all gene-paper records in PaperBLAST. The top 5 organisms (*H. sapiens*, *M. musculus*, *R. norvegicus*, *A. thaliana*, *D. melanogaster*) capture **72.8%**. Of 20,723 organisms with any literature, the top 1,000 capture 94.2%, leaving the remaining 19,723 organisms sharing just 5.8% of the literature.
heading: Finding 1: One organism dominates nearly half of all literature

text: Of 841K linked genes, 551K (65.6%) have one paper; the median is 1 and mean 3.8. The top 50 are human, and 6% of genes (50K) account for 57.7% of links.
quote: Of 841K genes with any text-mined paper link, **551K (65.6%)** have exactly 1 paper. The median is 1, the mean is 3.8. The top 50 most-referenced genes are all human — led by p53 (9,988 papers), TNF (6,002), and EGFR (5,895). Just 6% of genes (50K) account for 57.7% of all gene-paper links.
heading: Finding 2: 65.6% of genes have exactly one paper

text: The literature-coverage Gini coefficient is 0.967 for organisms and 0.669 for genes.
quote: For organisms, the Gini coefficient is **0.967** (where 1.0 is perfect inequality), indicating near-total concentration. For genes, the Gini is **0.669** — still very high. This mirrors wealth-inequality patterns in economics — a small fraction of biological entities receive nearly all research attention.
heading: Finding 3: Literature inequality is extreme — Lorenz curves

text: The top 100 of 15,312 bacterial organisms capture 44.3% of bacterial literature; the leading strains are M. tuberculosis H37Rv, E. coli K-12, and P. aeruginosa PAO1.
quote: Among 15,312 bacterial organisms, the top 100 capture **44.3%** of bacterial literature. The top 3 bacteria are all well-known pathogens or model organisms: *M. tuberculosis* H37Rv (9,079 papers), *E. coli* K-12 (8,860), and *P. aeruginosa* PAO1 (5,928). Environmental and non-pathogenic organisms are dramatically underrepresented.
heading: Finding 4: Bacterial research is concentrated on pathogens

text: The bacterial-literature analysis counts 15,312 bacterial organisms, whereas the domain table lists 5,997 Bacteria organisms. The report does not explain the differing populations or classifications.
quote: Among 15,312 bacterial organisms, the top 100 capture **44.3%** of bacterial literature.
heading: Finding 4: Bacterial research is concentrated on pathogens

text: MMseqs2 clustered 815,571 sequences into 628K clusters at 90% identity, 345K at 50%, and 215K at 30%. Large 50%-identity families include HSP70/BiP, GAPDH, enolase, and GroEL.
quote: MMseqs2 clustering of 815,571 PaperBLAST protein sequences at three identity thresholds reveals: **628K clusters at 90%** (77% — low strain-level redundancy), **345K at 50%** (protein family level), and **215K at 30%** (superfamily level). The largest families are housekeeping proteins: HSP70/BiP (650 members at 50%), GAPDH (609), enolase (552), GroEL (443).
heading: Finding 5: 345K protein families from 816K sequences

text: At 50% identity, 9.2% of families (31,653) have zero papers, 46.1% (159,046) have one, and 4.3% (14,904) have at least 20. The 5,218 multi-member families without literature contain 14,534 sequences.
quote: At 50% identity, **9.2% of protein families** (31,653) have **zero papers** across all members, and **46.1%** (159,046) have exactly 1 paper. Only **4.3%** of families (14,904) have 20 or more papers. 5,218 multi-member families — representing 14,534 sequences — have no literature whatsoever. These are the "dark" protein families.
heading: Finding 6: 55% of protein families are dark or dim

text: The PaperBLAST collection has 12.4 million rows across 14 tables, combining text-mined gene–paper links, annotations from 13 databases, and PDB structural data.
quote: contains **12.4 million rows** across 14 tables. The core data structure links genes to papers through text mining of PubMed Central full-text articles, supplemented by curated annotations from 13 databases and structural data from the PDB.
heading: Database Scale and Structure

text: Core table counts are 3,195,890 genepaper, 2,089,192 site, 1,951,949 snippet, 1,358,798 generif, 1,135,366 gene, 815,571 uniq, 599,587 curatedpaper, and 255,096 curatedgene rows.

heading: Database Scale and Structure

text: Paper coverage spans 1951–2026; 30.6% of records are from 2020 onward. There are 125,438 records from 22,271 papers in 2025 and 1,425 records from 2026; early-2026 snapshot timing is inferred.
quote: The database covers papers from **1951 to 2026**. Publications peak around 2020–2021, with 30.6% of records from 2020 onwards. The 2025 data includes 125,438 records from 22,271 papers. 1,425 records from 2026 are present, indicating the snapshot was taken in early 2026.
heading: Temporal Coverage

text: The prose reports 1.1M genes across 27,718 organisms but says Bacteria dominate organism count and Eukarya dominate gene count. Both rankings conflict with its domain table: Unknown has 14,798 organisms versus 5,997 Bacteria, and Bacteria has 397,544 genes versus 290,537 Eukarya.
quote: The 1.1M genes span 27,718 organisms across all domains of life. Bacteria dominate by organism count (6,000) but Eukarya dominate by gene count (291K) due to the massive over-representation of human and model organism genes. 14,798 organisms fell into an "Unknown" domain classification, indicating that the database includes many organisms not easily classified by name heuristics alone.
heading: Taxonomic Coverage

text: The domain table lists Bacteria at 5,997 organisms and 397,544 genes; Unknown at 14,798 and 397,511; Eukarya at 822 and 290,537; Virus at 5,730 and 27,199; and Archaea at 371 and 22,575. Its percentages are explicitly percentages of genes.
heading: Taxonomic Coverage

text: The report also gives 845K linked genes, 1.1M unique papers, and 3.2M associations; its earlier linked-gene count is 841K.
quote: 845K genes are linked to 1.1M unique papers via 3.2M many-to-many associations.
heading: Papers per Gene: The Many-to-Many Structure

text: 25.6% of gene-table genes (290K) lack a text-mined paper link, although curated or GeneRIF annotations remain.
quote: 25.6% of genes in the gene table (290K) have no text-mined paper link at all and rely solely on curated or GeneRIF annotations.
heading: Papers per Gene: The Many-to-Many Structure

text: SwissProt is the largest curated contributor, but PaperBLAST includes approximately 19% of its approximately 570K reviewed entries as of 2024. EcoCyc has 5.3 papers per protein.
quote: SwissProt contributes the most curated entries (110K proteins, 182K unique papers). PaperBLAST includes approximately 19% of the full SwissProt database (~570K reviewed entries as of 2024) — the subset that could be matched to PMC open-access literature. EcoCyc has the highest paper density per protein (5.3), reflecting its deep curation of *E. coli* metabolism.
heading: Curated Databases

text: The curated-database table gives exact protein counts, paper counts, and papers per protein for SwissProt, biolip, BRENDA, MetaCyc, and EcoCyc.
heading: Curated Databases

text: PaperBLAST has annotations for 132,179 PDB structures and 2.1M site records across four types. Its 48,991 unique ligands are led by zinc ions, chlorophyll A, calcium ions, and heme.
quote: PaperBLAST includes site annotations for **132,179 PDB structures** with 2.1M site records across 4 types: binding (1.69M), functional (182K), modified (112K), and mutagenesis (104K). The 48,991 unique ligands are topped by zinc ions (65K sites), chlorophyll A (58K), calcium ions (53K), and heme (44K).
heading: Structural Data

text: Singletons constitute 83.3% of clusters at 90% identity, 67.5% at 50%, and 62.8% at 30%; the largest 90%-identity cluster is actin with 212 members.
quote: At 90% identity, 83.3% of clusters are singletons — indicating that most PaperBLAST sequences are already non-redundant at the strain level. The largest 90% cluster is actin (212 members). At 50% identity, 67.5% are singletons; at 30%, 62.8%.
heading: Sequence Clustering

text: Protein family size is positively associated with literature coverage; the report states the direction of this relationship but gives no effect size here.
quote: There is a positive relationship between protein family size and literature coverage.
heading: Clustering and Literature: Larger Families Are Better Studied

text: At 50% identity, 95.4% of multi-member clusters have a paper-linked member, while 4.6% (5,218 families) do not; the report describes the latter as dominated by REBASE methyltransferases and biolip structural entries.
quote: 95.4% of multi-member 50% identity clusters have at least one member with a paper, but the remaining 4.6% (5,218 families) represent genuinely unstudied protein families. The "dark" families are dominated by REBASE methyltransferases and biolip structural entries — highly specialized proteins that lack published functional studies.
heading: Clustering and Literature: Larger Families Are Better Studied

text: Stoeger et al. (2018) are cited as external evidence for self-reinforcing, predictable human-gene research attention; this is context rather than a measurement from this analysis.
quote: **Stoeger et al. (2018)** showed that the most-studied human genes continue to attract the most new research, creating a self-reinforcing "rich-get-richer" dynamic. They demonstrated that gene attention can be predicted from a small set of chemical, physical, and biological properties — meaning the bias is systematic, not random.
heading: Literature Context

text: Perdigao et al. (2015) and Rocha et al. (2023) are cited as external dark-proteome and functional-unknomics context, distinct from this report's paper-count measurement.
quote: **Perdigao et al. (2015)**, who estimated that approximately 40% of protein residues fall in "dark" regions with no structural or functional information. Our finding that 55% of protein families at 50% identity have 0 or 1 papers extends this observation to the literature domain. **Rocha et al. (2023)** coined the term "functional unknomics" to describe the systematic study of conserved genes of unknown function, noting that significant and unexplored biology is encoded in the unstudied portion of genomes.
heading: Literature Context

text: The approximately 40% estimate concerns protein residues lacking structural or functional information; the report's 55% concerns 50%-identity families with 0 or 1 papers. Their denominators and definitions differ.
quote: **Perdigao et al. (2015)**, who estimated that approximately 40% of protein residues fall in "dark" regions with no structural or functional information. Our finding that 55% of protein families at 50% identity have 0 or 1 papers extends this observation to the literature domain.
heading: Literature Context

text: PaperBLAST is a protein-sequence-to-literature resource created by Price and Arkin in 2017, with subsequent interactive and curated annotation work.
quote: The PaperBLAST database itself was created by **Price & Arkin (2017)** specifically to address the challenge of connecting protein sequences to relevant literature. Their follow-up work on interactive tools for functional annotation (**Price & Arkin, 2024**) and Curated BLAST (**Price & Arkin, 2019**) further developed the approach of using literature text mining to aid gene function discovery.
heading: Literature Context

text: 129,823 VIMSS cross-references link PaperBLAST with the Fitness Browser, allowing literature coverage to be compared with experimental fitness phenotypes.
quote: The cross-database linkage analysis reveals that 129,823 VIMSS cross-references connect PaperBLAST to the Fitness Browser, creating a path from literature coverage to experimental fitness phenotypes — a resource for identifying functionally important but understudied genes.
heading: Novel Contribution

text: A text-mined paper mention does not establish functional characterization; some single-paper links may be incidental.
quote: **Text mining ≠ functional characterization**: A gene mentioned in a paper may be tangential to the study. The 65.6% with 1 paper likely includes many incidental mentions.
heading: Limitations

text: Mining only PubMed Central full text misses paywalled papers and can bias measured coverage by open-access rate.
quote: **PMC open-access only**: PaperBLAST only mines full-text from PubMed Central. Papers behind paywalls are missed, creating a systematic bias against fields/journals with lower open-access rates.
heading: Limitations

text: The report says heuristic mapping classified 35% of organisms as Unknown, but this conflicts with its table: Unknown contains 14,798 of 27,718 organisms, while 35.0% is the table's percentage of genes classified Unknown. Formal taxonomy lookup is proposed to improve accuracy.
quote: **Domain classification is approximate**: The heuristic organism-to-domain mapping classified 35% of organisms as "Unknown." A formal taxonomy lookup would improve accuracy.
heading: Limitations

text: The 50% sequence-identity definition of a protein family is conventional, not a universal biological boundary.
quote: **Clustering identity thresholds are arbitrary**: The 50% identity cutoff for "protein family" is conventional but does not correspond to a universal biological boundary.
heading: Limitations

text: Only 19% of SwissProt is represented in PaperBLAST; missing matching PMC full text is offered as a likely explanation, not demonstrated as the cause.
quote: **SwissProt coverage is partial**: Only 19% of SwissProt is in PaperBLAST, likely because many SwissProt entries lack matching PMC full-text. This means curated knowledge exists for many proteins that PaperBLAST cannot connect to.
heading: Limitations

text: Without negative controls, apparent lack of literature cannot be distinguished reliably from literature missed by text mining.
quote: **No negative controls**: We cannot easily distinguish genes that are genuinely unstudied from genes whose literature was missed by text mining.
heading: Limitations
